utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order for us to be able to follow, would the Prosecutor please tell us what book is this and exactly what portion of it because otherwise it's hard for us to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the exhibit number, but could she please tell us the title of the book so that we know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's Prosecution's Exhibit 90. It's the book that is written by Naser Oric, or allegedly written by Naser Oric. And this was the same exhibit that the Defence used yesterday, if that clarifies things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Just to help everyone, I think we have the page number in English. I just want you or wish you to repeat, Ms. Richardson, the page number in B/C/S, which I think is page 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, and that's in order to help Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I did say the page number, and it's my understanding it's page 29 as well, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In English it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In B/C/S it's page 29, in English page 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Karic, does that -- do you see that portion of the -- that I'm referring to that has the name Mirzet Garaljevic?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see the name at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you put on Sanction, please, the B/C/S version, if it is possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We're having a problem with Sanction at the moment. Just give me a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, as much as you require, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the usher ensure that the witness has page 59 in front of her because what confused me was that the Prosecutor said "page 29." That's what confused me, so it is possible that the same is happening with the witness now. It should be page 59 in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least check that or confirm that.

utterances.text: Because we've told the witness that it is page 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 29 is on the screen, which is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's the English text -- no, no, no, sorry. It's the B/C/S text. Yes -- but I don't know whether it's the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We're trying page 59. Ms. Vidovic may in fact be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you to Defence counsel for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So can you direct the witness again in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Karic, I am going to read from the portion -- it appears to be three lines down in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the portion: Mirzet Garaljevic was also arrested from his way back of military service from his village of Likari ... said that his son had been arrested and then set off for Sase and never came back. Ahmo Karic was arrested in Lasovac when he went there to get some food. I take it from your testimony that this is correct information, is it not, with respect to Mirzet Garaljevic but with respect to Ahmo Karic, your father?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this -- is this consistent with what you recall happening, that he was -- that your father was on the way to get food and he was arrested in your village?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. He was later released to go to Bare and Dimnici and to persuade his neighbours to surrender." Is that information in substance correct?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He went towards the forest, Bare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bare.

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't go to Dimnici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the part about Bare is correct? Was anyone sent to Dimnici with a message?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, before we were brought to the mine a man had been sent out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was sent to Dimnici or do you know or not?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sent to Dimnici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was sent with a message similar to the one taken by your father?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll read further down. "He never came back although his daughter Edina had stayed in the prison as a hostage. Begajeta Mujic from Lasovac had also been arrested and she appeared in Konjevic Polje one day in early June 1999 [as read], brought by Lieutenant Miroljub Todorovic to mediate with our resistance fighter the exchange of dead aggressors body left after the attack against Konjevic Polje." [as read] My question is: Well, we know that in fact you stayed and you were imprisoned and kept there. With respect to your aunt, do you -- you said that you don't know if she went to Konjevic Polje. Am I recalling your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was ordered to take a message to Konjevic Polje. And at that time, I didn't know whether she had ever reached Konjevic Polje or not because I was getting no information whatsoever. But the next day when she didn't come back, Commander Todorovic came in and said that Begajeta didn't show up at the time when she was told to come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later learn -- did you talk to her later about where it was that she went? Do you know later on after the war if you were able to speak to her during that time whether she went to Konjevic Polje? If you don't know, you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has already told you she doesn't know whether she went to Konjevic Polje or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, which is why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I was recalling her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What may be interesting to know is whether actually she disappeared from the world of the living that particular day on her way, or whether she was still alive at some later point in time, whether she's still alive today. That's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Karic, I take it you've heard Your Honour's questions. Is your aunt still alive?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she didn't come back, as stated here? She didn't come back to the detention facility in Sase?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just -- I'll get through this rather quickly at this point. Further down it states that -- yesterday you were asked about a particular portion of this book. It states: "A ring leaders were Novak Stjepanovic, a.k.a. Krke, from the hamlet of Jaruge near Kostanovci and Lieutenant Miroljub Todorovic. Miroljub, one of the first JNA officers that came forth to take part in ethnic cleansing, was commanding the battery in Sase, an outpost of the command in Bratunac." My question is in regards to Miroljub Todorovic. It's a fact, is it not, you testified that he was a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified to the fact that he was from Serbia and he was a commander and he was a member of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a commander, if he was a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second part of this -- this portion that I've read to you I would ask if he was in fact the commander of the Sase -- of the battery in Sase, of the place where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, it states that "the aggressor," which is the final sentence that I'm reading to you from this portion, "the aggressor units broke into the village of Poljak on the 25th -- 25th and 26th of May, 1992, killed a number of civilians and torched some of the houses. A larger massacre and torching spree was prevented by the resistance unit from Kragljivode." With respect to this information, do you know if in fact civilian houses were killed -- I'm sorry, civilians were killed and houses were torched from this particular village? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just one last question with respect to this portion. I probably should have read it out before, but it's a sentence which reads: "According to reliable sources, most of the detainees were killed and buried in the sludge deposit from the mine -- of the mine in Sase." Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe you also confirmed that this in fact did happen and that you -- you confirmed this information as it was stated in the book "Satan's son," which was Defence Exhibit 751. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A considerable number of civilians were supposed to have been taken away for an exchange, and only several people had been killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But yesterday when you were asked whether the information regarding the detainees being buried in the Sase mine area, you confirmed that that happened. So I guess what I'm seeking to find out from you is whether or not that particular sentence in this book is substantially correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday I specifically asked the witness about six detainees and not about the overall context and about the claim being made in the book that all sorts of people were buried there. So that's what the witness testified about and not the question put to her by Ms. Richardson. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the objection is a valid one, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't make a point about it, but it's my recollection that the exhibit was put to the witness. I would ask if this confirms what she knew. And the reason I raise it is only because the exhibit contained information that the witness had not particularly talked about. So what I'm seeking to find out now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a whole book.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a whole book.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, and the portion that was put to her was she confirmed what was she was told. And this portion of book contained very specific information about Krke and a portion about him with the hamlet, et cetera. In any event, Your Honour, it's really not that important. I'll just move on. Your Honour, if I could just have a moment, I think I may be at the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, Ms. Karic, you mentioned that Mr. -- Miroljub Todorovic was the commander of the mine and I believe you said he did -- how did he treat you? Did he treat you well?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He defended us. He defended us from the local Serbs I mean. He didn't participate in any rapes. He knew what was going on. He didn't put a stop to it, but in a way he saved us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you complained that you -- you had been raped, did he take any action in terms of trying to prevent that from happening?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you when we told him what had happened, he called the people who manned the ramp and he threatened them and said that Novak Stjepanovic, Krke, would be banned from the perimeter of the mine. But on the next day we saw him again, within the perimeter in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were not taken from that point on -- from that point on, after he spoke to the individuals, out to be raped again, were you?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I myself wasn't, but other girls were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. Okay, Your Honour, I don't have any other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two brief questions. Re-examined by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were shown an excerpt from the Prosecution document PP64 [as interpreted] which is a book by Mr. Besim Ibisevic and I would like the witness to be shown page 02930535 once again. And it's 564, the document P564. If you remember -- can you see the book in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look for the page 169 in the Bosnian version, which is page 19 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 169 in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have page 19 on Sanction, please, if possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the part that has to do with pre-war events and it has to do with a shootout in your area. And I'm going to read out two sentences to you. It says: "According to the indications of the newly arrived Serbs, those dances, there would be shots fired from firearms, explosions, or else there would be noise made by cars honking. Apparently the Serbs from the nearby villages were frightened and their representatives had asked us to go out in the field." Witness, can you please explain what it means supposedly -- supposedly frightened and concerned?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that it is not certain -- supposedly. It means that it is a supposition, an assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down below in the text there is a reference to a meeting and it says: "The meeting was held in one of the classrooms and there were the representatives of the local Serbs and the noisiest were Petko Rankic," and I would like to ask you whether Petko Rankic is the person you said was manning the ramp?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him at the time, was he armed? Was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was uniformed and he was armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you about somebody else. You were asked about Asim Redzic, a person from Srebrenica who used to work in the administrative building of the mine. Did you know any of the people from Srebrenica who used to work at the mine?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly in that you said that you knew the miners who worked inside the mine who were actually digging the hole inside with your father?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question. Mrs. Vojka Milovanovic, was it somebody whom you knew well before the war?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know her husband?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was Miko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll just back to this book for a moment, the bit that I've just quoted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this book, and this is the document P90, even if you don't have the book you will remember, it's 02919276, it's the part referring to your father, Ahmo Karic. It says: "Ahmo Karic was captured in Lasovac on the occasion when he came to collect some food, was allowed to go see his neighbours in Bare and Dimnici and relay a message to them to give themselves up." Is it true at all that your father was given a message to take to Dimnici or is Dimnici an all together village?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct at all. Dimnici is on the other side in relation to our village. It is further away from our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it mean that this information is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the information according to which your father was meant to be carrying a message to Dimnici, as stated in this book, is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: EDINA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Do you have any questions? Do you have any questions? I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I don't have any questions for the witness but in fact I would like to clear up this business of Akif Ustic being killed twice. Evidently there was a slight mistake in the translation. Number 4, it is Atif Ustic, number 6 is Akif Ustic, which is a -- different in the spelling of the first name. I'm looking at the B/C/S, Your Honour, number 4 and number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in the English translation it's Akif Ustic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It's clearly a mistake on our part in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Karic, we've come to the end of your testimony, and I am sure that you're happy that it is so. It means that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It means that very soon you will leave this courtroom. The -- our -- Madam Usher will escort you out of this courtroom, but before you leave us on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and on my own behalf, but also on behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for having been kind enough to come forward and give evidence as a Defence witness. You will, I can assure you, receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home at your earliest -- at the earliest opportunity. And on behalf of everyone present in this courtroom, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have got some matters to deal with before we adjourn to tomorrow. The other witness is not here to start, no, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: She, no, not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're going to make an effort to finish tomorrow, you said, both of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I thought on that subject I might say, Your Honour, that I'm planning to be no more than an hour and a half precisely so that we can finish with her tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And along the understanding, I mean, if it's possible to have such understanding, that we will be finished with her tomorrow. I wouldn't like to do all my utmost to be within an hour and a half and then find we go into Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. No, thanks. Now we have two matters to thresh. I take it, Ms. Richardson, in the meantime as you have made available or you were about to make available the three witness statements that Madam Vidovic referred to earlier on. Please go ahead. I think we're -- it's appropriate that they be entered in the records of the case, at least for the purpose that we need to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, I'm making it clear that what is contained in them will not constitute evidence for the purpose of the case against Naser Oric. Am I clear on this, Mr. Jones and Mr. Wubben? We are only going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Take cognisance of them only in relation to establishing whether they should have been disclosed under Rule 68(i), that's all. Rest we are not going to care about. In other words, they will not substitute in any way or supplement in any way the witness [sic] that Madam Karic gave here viva voce. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, for the record the Prosecution turned over during the break three witness statements to the Defence as well as to Your Honours. I'd like to put on record the translations that we have also turned -- attached to the original statement that was taken, firstly. The statement in B/C/S, that's ERN number 002181 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You will?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just tender them. Just tender them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure that you have copies in front of you. So I will enter the record and then ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. At this time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the first one, please. Let's take them one by one. I want the first statement in the original and with the translation, if available.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, so that there's no confusion, perhaps if I give you the ERN number and you can put it in, but I just want to make sure you're looking at the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, just give it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: For the English it's 00218 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, don't hurry, because I have to ... Yes, 0021.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's the first one?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's the first one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record the Prosecution at the request of the Trial Chamber has entered into the record the following document: In B/C/S a document consisting of three pages starting with ERN number 00218164 and ending with ERN 00218166, accompanied by the alleged -- allegedly corresponding translation into English or English translation consisting of a document of five pages -- of five pages. Bearing at the top of each page the same ERN numbers of the B/C/S document. So this is being marked as Trial Chamber document T -- it will be T what? TC or what?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: C4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: C4. C4. I am not marking them as a Prosecution exhibit so that we do not confuse them later on with the exhibits that we need for the purpose of our decision. The next document that is being tendered at the request of the Trial Chamber is the document which bears -- which in the B/C/S language consists of four pages starting with ERN 00223726 right up and inclusive of the page 00223729. Do I take it that you don't have an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. We do not have a translation of this at the moment, but one is -- we've requested one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So we should provide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document is not accompanied by a corresponding translation into English and is being marked as Trial Chamber document C5. Then we have the last -- and last document which is a four-page document, the first three of which are in handwritten format and the last being typed. They are all in B/C/S, and they start with ERN number 00355142 ending in 00355145, 5145. Together with this document the Prosecution is tendering a corresponding English translation of the -- what seems to be the handwritten part, and it consists in two pages numbered 1 and 2 with at the top of the right -- at the right-hand corner the indications of the ERN number of the corresponding part in B/C/S, that is 00355142 to 5144. This document is being marked as exhibit Court C6, C6. Are you happy with this mode of filing them or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is fine with this mode of filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, Ms. Vidovic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And if I may note that I had C5. I've already seen C5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. So, Ms. Vidovic, for the Defence, indicates that what is now Exhibit C5 she already was in possession of at the time of the examination-in-chief. We still require the translation in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have begun the process of the translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. With regard to C4, Ms. Vidovic, did you only become aware of it -- of its existence yesterday, C4 and C6?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for the clarification. This is precisely what we needed to know. We will of course in due course go through these amongst ourselves and we will come back to you if we need you to address this matter or if we require more information from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Richardson. And I also thank you, Ms. Vidovic. I am also informed, correct me if I'm wrong, that -- by my Legal Officer, that the Prosecution has approached the -- sorry, the Defence has approached the Prosecution to have made available -- to have available some documents which are required for an expert handwriting analysis. Is this correct? Is this information correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not that I doubt it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- but this is how it looks. So you confirm it, both of you? All right. So what is -- I know what the problem is but I would like you to state what the problem is. Yes, and I suppose the problem comes from your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, there is no problem as such. It's more the seeking of guidance from this Trial Chamber. This is a request towards us to give support of an examination by a forensic document examiner by the -- by the Defence -- from the Defence by letter of the 9th of September. And I received this letter on Monday, and on Wednesday I received the background, personal background, of this examiner. So we are looking into the matter and we will support the request. When we take a look at the request, we noticed that there are exhibits mentioned, a lot of P numbers, something like 27 P numbers, and also some documents referred to by ERN numbers. So apparently no documents that are tendered. But we have to find out anyhow, when it relates to exhibits already tendered into evidence, it means that it leaves the responsibility of the Prosecution as such from the Rules towards the registry, meaning also that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also the Trial Chamber because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And also the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because they are Court documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. And that's why whenever we support this request we want to include any implementation of any guidance or rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- By this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, fair enough. And I wouldn't think for a moment that there is divergence of this view on the part of the Defence. So let me tell you what I think, at least, should be done for the time being. I would prefer if the whole matter is formalised. In other words, since we have talking ultimately of a release of some documents for the purposes of forensic examination, I don't think that the matter can or should be handled exclusively between the parties without the intervention of the Trial Chamber. That's the first point that I should like to make. So what I suggest is the following: That if the Defence requires some documents -- both if they are already exhibited and it would also be the case if they are not in the records of the case, to be examined by a forensic expert. I think the matter should be referred to the Trial Chamber in a formal manner by means of an ad hoc motion indicating the following: The name of the expert that will be conducting the forensic examination and possibly with some basic information on how trustworthy he is. I mean, I'm not in any -- in any way hinting that he is not, but you will understand that we have responsibility here. Secondly, whether the examination will be held in the Netherlands or outside of the Netherlands. In either case, where it is going to be held. Thirdly, whether -- whether after consultation with your expert, Mr. Jones, Madam Vidovic, he requires to have the originals, originals, or the photocopies that exist in the records, because I would imagine that in the records we don't have the originals, we have photocopies, although we did see some originals at some point in time. So this is also a matter that you need to clarify for us. Right. Because the photocopies are in the records of the proceedings. The originals are not, as such, in the records of the proceedings, or at least some of them aren't that and that does make a little bit of a difference. And if the expert lives here in the Netherlands and he is going to conduct the test here in the Netherlands, whether it -- he would still require them outside the premises of this Tribunal or whether it would be fine -- equally fine with him if he came over and these documents are made available to him and photocopied by him or -- or whatever. Last but not least, I wish to make it clear that I would imagine that this is certainly not the first time that the matter has arisen before a Trial Chamber in this Tribunal. I must confess that it is the first time that it has arisen before me in this Tribunal. Not at home. At home, obviously, we have had this happen and we make them available, we make the original available against certified copies, receipts, and everything. But what I am trying to tell you is: This being so I would inquire what the normal practice of the Tribunal is in consultation with the registrar. I want to know exactly how this has been handled before. And in as far as we will believe that it is compatible with the rights of the accused and also the security of -- and chain of custody of these documents, we will try to keep the -- the system that should already I suppose be in place. This is our position for the time being. Obviously we can -- we will come back to you, but I would suggest, Mr. Jones, that since time is flying that you follow-up with a motion straight away. And this matter you will have time to consult amongst yourself and also with the registrar. I will do the same and then I will consult with my two colleagues on which way -- best to go about it. But what I can assure you is that you can receive all the assistance that you require to make it possible for your expert to conduct whatever forensic analysis you think is necessary. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. For the Prosecution this sounds very productive and we'll speed it -- but also be very clear and transparent procedure as an outcome. And in order to avoid any reply to a motion and respond further, I would ask that the Defence also give a thought about the presence of someone from the Prosecution whenever the documents, those original documents, are examined. The second issue is, whenever it is outside the premises of the Tribunal examined, if it is possible whether or not to examine it at Dutch Forensic Institute in Rijswijk but -- by this examiner, of course. And the third issue, any assistance of the chain of custody practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are two -- I thank you for these three points. I don't agree, or I definitely cannot follow you up on the second point. The last thing I would do is to indicate to the Defence where ideally they should conduct the forensic examination, that's up to them. As much as I cannot indicate to them who should conduct these examinations, I do concede without -- or I do concede hands down that the fact that there may be originals which are in possession as Prosecution, Office of the Prosecution, which are not in the records of the case. We will have to take certain precautions. And equally, we have to take certain precautions as records the records of the case because the -- both the registry aspect and the Trial Chamber aspect have to be safeguarded. That's all. But I don't think there should be any -- any difficulties there. Yes, Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones, do you have any comments or is it clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will be very clear in our motion, which I hope shall be completed by tomorrow, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you. Although we will not be sitting next week, we will all be here to deal with the matter. I'm going to be here all the time so there will be a decision on it in the course of next week, if there are no problems. All right. Okay. I think we have covered the totality of the matters that we had. I will be signing the Rule 92 bis decision now, as soon as I get out of this courtroom. It's ready. I do wish to remind you that you still owe us your reaction to the response on the Prosecution on the Rule 70 business - I don't need to hear anything now - and that you're supposed to file your response with regard to the -- the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Witness protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the witness protection question. When are due -- when are we expected?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We plan to file today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's perfect. In that case, in that case, we will probably be dealing with it in the course of next week. All right. Anything you want to raise before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for your cooperation. I also thank everyone else. We stand adjourned until tomorrow when we will start hearing the testimony of the next witness. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of September, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 25
